name: Diego Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Diego, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small workers' co-op that does energy retrofits, which means making old houses warmer and cheaper to heat. Most days we're in a terraced house from about 1900, and I'm building loft floors, boxing in pipes for the heat pump, and fixing battens on the outside walls for insulation boards. I'm the junior, at fifty-eight, which makes the young ones laugh.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there at your age?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran a bike repair shop for twenty years until online shops and those cheap e-bikes finished it in 2021. I'd always fixed things, so I went to the co-op and said I'll carry, sweep, anything, teach me. My carpentry is still rough, honestly, but I'm the one who sorts out the tech for everybody.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you mean by sorting out the tech?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take a photo of a loft on my phone, and the AI gives me a rough cutting list, so we buy the right amount of timber. I use it to translate for Andrei, who's Romanian and much better with a saw than me. Every day I find a new trick, and Rosa, who runs the jobs, says I'm the co-op's unofficial computer department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a bit of a let-down, but fine, we've got houses to fix. I'd probably post that the real revolution we need is warm homes, not smart robots, and the money should go there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things stay as they are, and they're not bad. I'll keep being the junior with the clever phone, and maybe in a few years I'll be a decent carpenter too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I use now, the cutting lists, the translation, the photos of damp. I'd ask Rosa to send me on the airtightness course in spring, that's sealing the gaps so heat doesn't leak out. And I'd keep putting my bit into savings, we've got about two and a half months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, slightly disappointed, the way you feel when a film is overhyped. But relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said disappointed. What did you hope AI would do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hoped it would design a whole retrofit in one go, measure the house, plan the heat pump, order the boards. That would let us do twice as many houses for the same people. Plenty of folk are cold this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena make of this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's a librarian, and she'd be pleased, she's always said the hype was like the dot-com bubble. She'd say, Diego, you can stop reading about robots in bed now.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down but we've got houses to fix. I'd post that the revolution we need is warm homes, not smart robots, and the money should go there.
S0.think: Privately things staying the same is fine for me. I'd stay the junior with the clever phone and maybe become a decent carpenter in a few years.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for cutting lists, translation and damp photos, and asks to go on the airtightness course in spring. Keeps adding to savings of about two and a half months.
S0.feel: Calm, a little disappointed like after an overhyped film.
S0.quote: Diego, you can stop reading about robots in bed now.
S0.fieldNote: Diego is unusual: a late-career junior who's the most tech-confident person on his crew. His disappointment is real because he saw AI as a way to warm more homes. He frames everything through the co-op's purpose rather than his own pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news if the workers own the machines. In a co-op, if a tool saves us a day, that day is ours to use on another house, not a reason to sack someone. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me personally. I'm not the best with a saw, but I'm the best on the crew with the new stuff. If more of the job becomes planning, scanning and running machines, I go from junior to useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Rosa to try a laser scanner that maps a house and an AI that plans the insulation, and I'd volunteer to run it. I'd do an online course on retrofit design in the evenings. And I'd organise a session where I show the others the tools, so nobody gets left behind, especially Andrei.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. I'd be careful not to sound too excited in front of the older guys, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who's sixty-three and the best joiner I know. He won't touch a phone, and he'd feel like the world had moved past him. I'd want him teaching the young ones joinery while I do the gadgets, so we need each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're too optimistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I said the same about e-bikes when I had the shop, I thought I'd fix them, and instead they killed me. So yes, I've been wrong before, and I try to remember it.

S1.say: I'd say this is good news if workers own the machines. In a co-op, a tool that saves a day means another house done, not someone sacked.
S1.think: Privately it's good for me, because I'm the best on the crew with new tools even if I'm weak with a saw. If the job becomes planning, scanning and machines, I go from junior to useful.
S1.do: Pushes the co-op to try a laser scanner and AI insulation planning, and volunteers to run them. Takes an evening retrofit design course and runs a session teaching the crew the tools.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, though he hides the excitement from older colleagues.
S1.quote: I said the same about e-bikes when I had the shop, I thought I'd fix them, and instead they killed me.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as a promotion. What makes him credible is that he admits he misread e-bikes and lost his shop. He pairs himself with the older joiner rather than replacing him, which fits his co-op values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-ops and the public should own these machines, not three companies in California. If AGI arrives in two years, the question isn't jobs, it's who owns the robots. I'd say it at the co-op meeting, on every forum, and I'd go to the protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried but also curious. I'd be sixty, and I'm not daft, a junior carpenter is the easiest thing to replace. But if the co-op could buy a robot together, maybe I'm the one who runs it, and that's still a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the co-op to put a vote on buying a building robot as soon as they're for sale, and I'd put my name down to learn it. I'd keep a month of savings back for emergencies and put the rest into the co-op as a member loan for the robot. And I'd join the campaign for public ownership of AI, I'd actually knock on doors for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous in the stomach, but awake. I'd feel more alive than scared, which might be stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put your savings into the co-op. What does Lena say about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say absolutely not, at first. Then we'd argue in the kitchen until midnight, and we'd probably agree on half. Her library would be shutting too, so she'd want something that's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Mateo, your son, who works in software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. He tests software, and an AI that can do any job can surely test itself. I'd tell him to come and learn the co-op work with me, and he'd laugh, but maybe not for long.

S2.say: I'd say co-ops and the public should own these machines, not three companies. If AGI arrives in two years, the real question is who owns the robots, and I'd say it at protests and on every forum.
S2.think: Privately I'd be worried but curious. A sixty-year-old junior carpenter is easy to replace, but if the co-op bought a robot together, I might be the one running it.
S2.do: Asks the co-op to vote on buying a building robot and signs up to learn it. Keeps a month of savings for emergencies and lends the rest to the co-op, and knocks on doors for public ownership of AI.
S2.feel: Nervous but awake, more alive than scared, which he suspects might be foolish.
S2.quote: If AGI arrives in two years, the question isn't jobs, it's who owns the robots.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture his first move is collective ownership, and he'd risk his own savings on it. The worry he can't plan around is his son in software. His argument with Lena, ending in a likely compromise, felt very real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but with five years I'd say we can build the co-ops and the rules properly. I'd go to the council and ask for public money to help small builders buy robots together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I think I'd be fine. By 2031 I'd be sixty-three, and I'd have spent the time learning to run the machines. I'd also be close enough to the end that I could step back if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a robotics operator course as soon as there's one, probably at the technical college. I'd put a hundred a month into a co-op fund for equipment, and keep the rest in savings. And I'd make Mateo's plan a family project, sitting down with him every few weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a fair way. I know there's time, but I know time goes fast at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's one specific thing you'd want to master by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching a robot to work on a crooked old house. New-builds are easy, everything's straight. Our houses from 1900 have walls that lean like drunks, and someone has to tell the machine what's going on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd feel more alive than scared in the fast picture. Is that true here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Here it's less exciting and more sensible. Honestly I prefer this one, even if I'd never admit it on the forum. Exciting is for people with more than two months saved.

S3.say: I'd give the same message but say five years is time to build co-ops and rules properly. I'd ask the council for public money to help small builders buy robots together.
S3.think: Privately I think I'd be fine with five years. I'd be sixty-three in 2031, skilled at running the machines, and near enough to the end to step back if needed.
S3.do: Takes a robotics operator course at the technical college as soon as one exists. Puts a hundred a month into a co-op equipment fund, keeps the rest saved, and makes a plan with his son every few weeks.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a fair way, knowing time moves fast at his age.
S3.quote: Exciting is for people with more than two months saved.
S3.fieldNote: He admits privately that he prefers the slower picture to the dramatic one, a gap from his public enthusiasm. His idea of skill is very specific: guiding robots through crooked old houses. His son's future remains the main thread of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years, so let's make every house warm and every robot shared. I'd say that's the decade we get to choose what kind of country we live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a gift for me. I'd be sixty-eight, retired from the co-op, and I'd have helped bring the machines in, which I'd love. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, learning the tools as they come, and push the co-op to plan for 2036 now. I'd keep saving normally. And I'd probably start a small evening class for older trades people who want to learn AI, because I know how scary it looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite happy, actually. Like being given a long runway for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you call your evening class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like Old Hands, New Tools. Pete would refuse to come, then turn up in week three and pretend he was passing by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that does bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo and his generation. Ten years is fine for me, but for him it's half his career. I'd want him to spend it well, and I can't do it for him.

S4.say: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years, so let's make every house warm and every robot shared. It's a decade to choose what kind of country we live in.
S4.think: Privately ten years is a gift. I'd be sixty-eight and retired, having helped bring the machines into the co-op, and I'd sleep fine.
S4.do: Keeps working and learning new tools as they arrive, and pushes the co-op to plan for 2036 now. Saves at his usual rate and starts an evening class teaching AI to older trades people.
S4.feel: Calm and happy, like being given a long runway for once.
S4.quote: Pete would refuse to come, then turn up in week three and pretend he was passing by.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Diego looks forward to retiring after helping bring machines in, and he turns his tech confidence into teaching others. His only real worry is his son's career. The timing makes the biggest difference to his mood.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mainly for Mateo and for people like Pete who won't touch the tools. What would help is public money for co-ops and small builders to own the machines, and free courses for older workers that actually start where we are.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want a robot on my crew. I would, if it was ours. A robot owned by us is a colleague, and a robot owned by someone else is a boss.

headlineQuote: A robot owned by us is a colleague, and a robot owned by someone else is a boss.
portrait: Diego is a fifty-eight-year-old former bike shop owner who joined an energy retrofit co-op as its junior carpenter and quickly became its unofficial computer department. He uses AI every day for cutting lists and translation, and sees most change through the question of who owns the machines. Steady change looks like a promotion to him, while two-year AGI makes him anxious but energised, ready to lend his savings to buy a co-op robot. With five or ten years he relaxes, and his worry turns to his son's software career and older colleagues who won't touch the tools.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mostly for his son Mateo and for older colleagues like Pete who won't use new tools.
whatWouldHelp: Public money so co-ops and small builders can own the machines, and free courses for older workers that start where they are.
